query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small Hf content (approximately 0.5 atomic %) to the base refractory high‐entropy alloy will form finely dispersed Hf-rich precipitates that inhibit grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby increasing the alloy’s high-temperature yield strength and ductility without degrading its room‐temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1 alloy) fabricated by standard melting and thermomechanical processing that shows acceptable room-temperature performance but limited high-temperature mechanical capability.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.5 at% hafnium into the alloy composition during melting so that, upon cooling and subsequent thermomechanical treatment, Hf-rich precipitates form at grain boundaries and within the strengthening B2 matrix.
generation.conditions: The alloys are produced under identical processing conditions (e.g., arc melting followed by controlled thermomechanical processing). Their performance is evaluated by tensile tests conducted at high temperatures relevant for jet-turbine service (for example, in the range of 800–1000 °C) as well as at room temperature, with all other variables (e.g., overall composition, cooling rates) held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely distributed Hf-rich precipitates that form along grain boundaries and within the matrix of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates act as obstacles for grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion during high-temperature deformation, thus enhancing yield strength and ductility under elevated temperatures while leaving the room-temperature deformation mechanisms largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Hf-free alloy, the Hf-modified alloy is expected to exhibit an increase in high-temperature tensile yield strength and ductility (improvements on the order of 30–50% have been observed in comparable alloys) with little to no change in room-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The Hf-free refractory high-entropy alloy processed under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This performance improvement is anticipated for the specific alloy system and processing route described; it is valid under the prescribed high-temperature tensile (e.g., 800–1000 °C) and room-temperature test conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement magnitude depends on precise Hf distribution and processing parameters; deviations in Hf content or nonuniform precipitate formation could lead to unexpected brittle phase formation or a different strengthening response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys that are identical in all respects except for the Hf addition: one set with 0.5 at% Hf and one control set without Hf. Process both sets via the same melting and thermomechanical route. Evaluate microstructure (to confirm the formation of Hf-rich precipitates) using microscopy techniques and perform tensile tests at both room temperature and a high temperature (e.g., 800–1000 °C).
measurements: Microstructural analysis (phase identification and precipitate distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength and ductility over the control, or if its room-temperature performance is degraded, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged.
